chunks: When a motor or solenoid draws least current. The question: When does a motor/solenoid draw the least amount of current?
A DC motor draws the least current when it spins freely at its top speed with nothing to push against.
By then its own back-EMF almost cancels the supply voltage, so only a small current is left to overcome friction.
A solenoid draws no current when it is off, and the smallest useful current is a low holding current once it has pulled in.
Imagine pedaling a bike on a smooth flat road at your top speed. You barely push, just enough to beat the friction and the wind. Add a hill or a headwind and you must push harder.
A free-running motor is in that easy state. If something pushes the bike downhill faster than you can pedal, the bike pushes you, and the motor can even act as a generator.
Current falls linearly with speed. The line would reach zero at the ideal speed V over K e = 600 rad/s (grey line), but friction demands 0.
5 amps, so a real free-running motor settles at 575 rad/s (orange line).
Beyond 600 rad/s the line goes negative: the motor is being driven by the load and pushes current back to the supply.
No-load speed: the speed a motor reaches when it has no mechanical load.
Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates, close to the supply at no load ("When a motor or solenoid draws most current").
Friction and windage: the small drag from bearings and air that a free-running motor still overcomes. Holding current: the lower current that keeps a solenoid pulled in.
PWM: switching the voltage on and off quickly so the average voltage and current are lower.
With a 12 volts supply and a 1 ohms motor, the current at stall is 12 amps. At no load, the back-EMF is about 11. 5 volts, so the current is (12 minus 11. 5) over 1 equals 0.
5 amps. A 24 volts, 48 ohms solenoid draws 24 over 48 equals 0. 5 amps and 12 watts while on. Once pulled in, switching it with 20% PWM cuts the average current to 0. 2 times 0.
5 equals 0. 1 amps, and the power to about 0. 48 watts (current squared times resistance, because the coil smooths the current). That is the whole idea.

"For a motor, the steady-state minimum is at no load and top speed: the back-EMF almost equals the supply, so the current is just what's needed to overcome friction, about half an amp versus 12 amps at stall in my example.
The absolute minimum is the instant of turn-on, when the inductor makes the current start at zero.
If the shaft is driven faster than no-load speed, the current goes negative: regeneration. For a solenoid it's zero when off, or the small PWM hold current once it has pulled in."
